en: Title: Sattvārādhanastava Author: Nāgārjuna Source: Cheung 2025
Devotion to the welfare of sentient beings alone is my devotion; any other is not devotion.
Devotion, however, consists in that [state] wherein he does not abandon his compassion for me.
For one who wanders having abandoned compassion, whatever lapses there may be, it is compassion alone that ought to uplift them, and nothing else. (1)
Therefore I have been honored by him, he who bears the burden of my teaching, whose activity toward sentient beings proceeds out of a following of compassion,
and who possesses ethical discipline, learning, compassion, and keen intelligence.
Whoever possesses [this] has indeed always honored the Sugata.
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, I have attained perfection;
it is solely for the welfare of sentient beings that I bear this body.
For how can he who slays sentient beings even in his mind take refuge in me, since he is indifferent toward me?
Yet that worship which brings benefit to sentient beings, though it be slight, is true worship.

That worship which brings satisfaction to the mind of the one worthy of honor does not fail to reach the object of honor, even if it is performed with ritual refinement; however, worship that is violent in nature or arises from the intent to harm another does not reach the one worthy of honor, even if it is well-prepared.
Wives, sons, wealth, and even a great kingdom, as well as flesh, blood, fat, eyes, and the body itself—
whatever things I have renounced for the sake of what is dear.
Whoever harms them, by him I am harmed;
for my supreme worship consists in benefiting sentient beings,
and doing harm to sentient beings is my defeat.
Suffering and happiness are desired by me as equal for all beings; how can he who strikes at beings be mine?
Having encountered beings, I have performed virtuous deeds and propitiated the Protectors.
The perfections were attained by one who extended the welfare of the assembly of beings;
with a mind exerted for the sake of beings, the power of Māra was broken;
and beings themselves have acted in such various ways that I have been made a Buddha. (7)

Toward what object should compassion and loving-kindness be established here; toward what should they be directed, and where should equanimity and sympathetic joy be applied? Toward what objective domain should the liberations and so forth be directed? For whose sake was patience cultivated for so long by you with a mind devoted to compassion?
If living beings were not my friends in the performance of what is dear throughout birth after birth,

then these very beings— having attained the state of elephants and other forms— would have been given by me many times; and these very beings, having become worthy recipients, would have been made to accept what was to be given by me.
Since it is through sentient beings alone that my compassion has increased by their undergoing various states of existence,

if I do not protect those very beings, for whose sake would any purpose have been accomplished? If there were no living creatures in this saṃsāra, which is so full of calamities and blows, [what would there be to protect?]

For what purpose was this incomparable mockery of the whirlpool of birth made one's own, and for whose sake was this most wonderful majesty of the Sugata— the ornament of the world— sought, were sentient beings not dear to me? (10)
"As long as this teaching of mine, which illuminates the world, endures, so long must you— who are self-possessed and devoted to the welfare of others— remain.
And having heard my well-practiced conduct again and again, you must remain untiring for the sake of sentient beings."
Nor should those who carry this body, which is devoid of essence, feel weary.
The Mahāyāna sūtra entitled *Sattvārādhana*, spoken by the Perfectly Awakened One, is completed.
